claim: PKM2 expression is significantly increased in NK cells from mice that received poly(I:C) compared to control mice.
source: There was a significant increase in the expression of PKM2 in NK cells from mice that received poly(I:C) as measured by flow cytometry (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1a comparing PKM2 expression in NK cells from poly(I:C)-treated versus control mice.

claim: PKM2 protein and mRNA expression increases over time following IL-2/IL-12 activation, peaking at 24 hours post-stimulation.
source: The expression of PKM2 increased over time following activation peaking at 24 hr post cytokine stimulation (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and rtPCR data shown in Figure 1b measuring PKM2 expression at multiple time points after IL-2/IL-12 stimulation.

claim: mTORC1 is active in NK cells stimulated in vivo following poly(I:C) injection and in IL-2/IL-12 stimulated NK cells.
source: The mammalian Target of Rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) has been shown to be active both in NK cells stimulated in vivo following poly(I:C) injection, and in IL-2/IL-12 stimulated NK cells, and is an important regulator of NK cell metabolism (Donnelly et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Donnelly et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 activity using rapamycin significantly reduces PKM2 mRNA and protein abundance in IL-2/12 stimulated cultured NK cells.
source: Inhibition of mTORC1 activity using the inhibitor rapamycin significantly reduced the abundance of PKM2 mRNA and protein in IL-2/12 stimulated cultured NK cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 1c comparing PKM2 expression in rapamycin-treated versus control NK cells.

claim: Pkm1 mRNA is expressed and regulated by mTORC1 in IL-2/12 stimulated NK cells.
source: Similarly, we confirmed that Pkm1 mRNA is expressed and regulated by mTORC1 in IL-2/12 stimulated NK cells along with PKM1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: NK cells do not express the liver- and erythrocyte-specific isoforms of pyruvate kinase, PK-L and PK-R.
source: Although we were primarily concerned with the pyruvate kinase muscle (PKM) family of enzymes, we also confirmed that NK cells do not express the liver- and erythrocyte-specific isoforms of pyruvate kinase, PK-L and PK-R respectively, using quantitative proteomics.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data showing no detectable peptides from the Pklr gene.

claim: IL-2/12 stimulated NK cells contain upwards of 6 × 10^6 copies of PKM peptide with no detectable peptides from the Pklr gene.
source: We observed upwards of 6 × 106 copies of PKM peptide in IL-2/12 stimulated NK cells, with no detectable peptides from the Pklr gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: PKM2 is ninefold more abundant than PKM1 in cytokine activated NK cells.
source: Interestingly, quantitative proteomics analysis revealed that PKM2 is ninefold more abundant than PKM1 in cytokine activated NK cells (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 1d comparing PKM1 and PKM2 protein copy numbers.

claim: IL-2/12-stimulated NK cells express both monomeric and tetrameric PKM2.
source: Western blotting revealed that IL-2/12-stimulated NK cells express both monomeric and tetrameric PKM2 (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by DSS crosslinking and western blot data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: PKM2 expression is robustly increased in activated NK cells.
source: Therefore, PKM2 expression is robustly increased in activated NK cells, is the dominant pyruvate kinase isoform in these metabolically active cells and is present as both monomers and tetramers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results presented in Figure 1.

claim: PKM2 is the dominant pyruvate kinase isoform in metabolically active NK cells.
source: Therefore, PKM2 expression is robustly increased in activated NK cells, is the dominant pyruvate kinase isoform in these metabolically active cells and is present as both monomers and tetramers.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data showing PKM2 is ninefold more abundant than PKM1.

claim: NK cells containing both the Ncr1-Cre transgene and homozygous for the Pkm2fl locus specifically excise exon 10 of the Pkm2 gene.
source: The data show that NK cells containing both the Ncr1-Cre transgene and homozygous for the Pkm2fl locus specifically excise the exon 10 of Pkm2 gene leading to a smaller DNA band (~200 kb) (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR and gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: NK cells developed normally in Pkm2NK-KO mice as the numbers and frequencies of NK cells and NK cell subsets were normal in the spleen compared to control Pkm2NK-WT mice.
source: NK cells developed normally in Pkm2NK-KO mice as the numbers and frequencies of NK cells and NK cells subsets were normal in the spleen when compared to control Pkm2NK-WT mice (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b,c comparing NK cell populations in Pkm2NK-KO versus Pkm2NK-WT mice.

claim: Splenic Pkm2NK-KO NK cells expanded normally ex vivo in response to low-dose IL-15.
source: Consistent with normal NK cell development splenic Pkm2NK-KO NK cells expanded normally ex vivo in response to low-dose IL-15, important for NK cells homeostatic proliferation (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2d comparing expansion of Pkm2NK-KO versus Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.

claim: Pkm2NK-KO NK cells expressed comparable levels of granzyme B to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells following IL-2/IL-12 stimulation.
source: Pkm2NK-KO NK cells expressed comparable levels of the cytotoxic granule component granzyme B and produced equivalent amounts of IFNγ compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 2e–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2e–f comparing granzyme B expression.

claim: Pkm2NK-KO NK cells produced equivalent amounts of IFNγ compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells following IL-2/IL-12 stimulation.
source: Pkm2NK-KO NK cells expressed comparable levels of the cytotoxic granule component granzyme B and produced equivalent amounts of IFNγ compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 2e–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2g–h comparing IFNγ production.

claim: There were no differences in the secretion of cytokines (IFNγ, TNFα and IL-10) or chemokines (MIP1α and MIP1β) between stimulated Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: Additionally, there were no differences in the secretion of cytokines (IFNγ, TNFα and IL-10) or chemokines (MIP1α and MIP1β) between stimulated Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytometric bead array data shown in Figure 2i,j comparing cytokine and chemokine secretion.

claim: The spleen size as determined by weight was equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice 4 days post-MCMV infection.
source: The spleen size as determined by weight was equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice as were the numbers of NK cells and the frequencies of Ly49H+ splenic NK cells (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by spleen weight measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The numbers of NK cells were equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice 4 days post-MCMV infection.
source: The spleen size as determined by weight was equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice as were the numbers of NK cells and the frequencies of Ly49H+ splenic NK cells (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The frequencies of Ly49H+ splenic NK cells were equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice 4 days post-MCMV infection.
source: The spleen size as determined by weight was equivalent in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice as were the numbers of NK cells and the frequencies of Ly49H+ splenic NK cells (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There was no difference in NK cell activation in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice based on CD69 expression 4 days post-MCMV infection.
source: In addition, there was no difference in NK cell activation in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice based on CD69 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3d–e.

claim: Ly49H+ cells from Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice showed equivalent levels of virus-induced proliferation based on BrDU incorporation 4 days post-MCMV infection.
source: Additionally, Ly49H+ cells from these mice showed equivalent levels of virus-induced proliferation based on BrDU incorporation (Figure 3d–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by BrDU incorporation data shown in Figure 3f–g.

claim: There were no differences in the levels of IFNγ, TNFα and IL10 in the serum of uninfected or MCMV infected Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice.
source: There were no differences in the levels of IFNγ, TNFα and IL10 in the serum of uninfected or MCMV infected Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytometric bead array data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Viral loads on day 4 post-MCMV infection were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice.
source: Finally, viral loads on day 4 were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT mice (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data for viral load shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The immune response to MCMV infection was not compromised in mice containing Pkm2 deficient NK cells 4 days post-infection.
source: These data clearly show that the immune response to MCMV infection was not compromised in mice containing Pkm2 deficient NK cells 4 days post-infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple measurements of immune parameters shown in Figure 3.

claim: The basal and maximal rates of glycolysis were comparable in both unstimulated and IL2/IL12 stimulated Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: The basal and maximal rates of glycolysis and of OXPHOS were comparable in both unstimulated and IL2/IL12 stimulated Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data shown in Figure 4a–e.

claim: The basal and maximal rates of OXPHOS were comparable in both unstimulated and IL2/IL12 stimulated Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: The basal and maximal rates of glycolysis and of OXPHOS were comparable in both unstimulated and IL2/IL12 stimulated Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data shown in Figure 4a–e.

claim: The levels of glycolytic intermediates were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: In addition, the levels of glycolytic intermediates, pentose phosphate pathway components (PPP) and elements of the tricarboxcylic acid (TCA) cycle were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The levels of pentose phosphate pathway components were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: In addition, the levels of glycolytic intermediates, pentose phosphate pathway components (PPP) and elements of the tricarboxcylic acid (TCA) cycle were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The levels of tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle elements were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: In addition, the levels of glycolytic intermediates, pentose phosphate pathway components (PPP) and elements of the tricarboxcylic acid (TCA) cycle were similar in Pkm2NK-KO and Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Expression of PKM1 was significantly increased in Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: Indeed, RNA and protein analyses using rtPCR, RNAseq and western blotting revealed that expression of PKM1, the alternative splice variant of Pkm2, was significantly increased in Pkm2NK-KO compared to Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 4i–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by rtPCR, RNAseq, and western blot data shown in Figure 4i–k.

claim: Pkm2NK-KO NK cells had precisely compensated with increased PKM1 expression to maintain an extraordinarily similar rate of overall pyruvate kinase activity.
source: Remarkably, Pkm2NK-KO NK cells had precisely compensated with increased PKM1 expression to maintain an extraordinarily similar rate of overall pyruvate kinase activity, as measured using a direct biochemical enzymatic assay (Figure 4l).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyruvate kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: There were very few significant differentially expressed genes in the transcriptome of Pkm2NK-KO versus Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: There were very few significant differentially expressed genes (DEG) in the transcriptome of Pkm2NK-KO versus Pkm2NK-WT NK cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There were only two genes upregulated by over twofold and four genes downregulated by greater than twofold expression with a false discovery rate of 0.05 in Pkm2NK-KO versus Pkm2NK-WT NK cells.
source: There were only two genes upregulated by over twofold and four genes downregulated by greater than twofold expression with a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 5a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was no enrichment for HIF1α target genes in the differentially expressed mRNA in Pkm2NK-KO NK cells.
source: Importantly, there was no enrichment for HIF1α or STAT5 target genes in the differentially expressed mRNA in Pkm2NK-KO NK cells (Figure 5b and c, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of HIF1α targets shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There was no enrichment for STAT5 target genes in the differentially expressed mRNA in Pkm2NK-KO NK cells.
source: Importantly, there was no enrichment for HIF1α or STAT5 target genes in the differentially expressed mRNA in Pkm2NK-KO NK cells (Figure 5b and c, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of STAT5 targets shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TEPP-46 is a pharmacological activator of PKM2 function that promotes the oligomerisation of mono/dimeric PKM2 into tetrameric, catalytically active PKM2.
source: TEPP-46 is a pharmacological activator of PKM2 function that promotes the oligomerisation of mono/dimeric PKM2 into tetrameric, catalytically active PKM2 (Anastasiou et al., 2012), resulting in the loss of non-glycolytic PKM2 signalling functions (Angiari et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anastasiou et al., 2012 and Angiari et al., 2020.

claim: TEPP-46 treatment results in the loss of non-glycolytic PKM2 signalling functions.
source: TEPP-46 is a pharmacological activator of PKM2 function that promotes the oligomerisation of mono/dimeric PKM2 into tetrameric, catalytically active PKM2 (Anastasiou et al., 2012), resulting in the loss of non-glycolytic PKM2 signalling functions (Angiari et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Angiari et al., 2020.

claim: There were only 10 differentially expressed genes with a fold change cutoff of 2 and a FDR of 0.05 between IL-2/IL-12 stimulated NK cells treated with TEPP-46 versus vehicle.
source: The transcriptomes were remarkably similar between the two conditions with only 10 DEG with a fold change cutoff of 2 and a FDR of 0.05 (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: There was no enrichment for HIF1α target genes in TEPP-46 treated NK cells aside from a small but significant increase in Bcl2 expression.
source: Amongst these genes, there was again no enrichment for HIF1α or STAT5 targets aside from a small but significant increase in Bcl2 expression (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: There was no enrichment for STAT5 target genes in TEPP-46 treated NK cells aside from a small but significant increase in Bcl2 expression.
source: Amongst these genes, there was again no enrichment for HIF1α or STAT5 targets aside from a small but significant increase in Bcl2 expression (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: PKM2 is not necessary for the regulation of the NK cell transcriptome.
source: Therefore, using both genetic and pharmacological approaches these data clearly show that PKM2 is not necessary for the regulation of the NK cell transcriptome.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNAseq data from both Pkm2NK-KO cells and TEPP-46 treated cells showing minimal transcriptional changes.

claim: Addition of TEPP-46 for 1 hr to cultured NK cells that had been previously stimulated for 18 hr with IL-2/IL-12 resulted in an increase in pyruvate kinase activity.
source: As expected, addition of TEPP-46 for 1 hr to cultured NK cells that had been previously stimulated for 18 hr with IL-2/IL-12, resulted in an increase in pyruvate kinase activity and of cellular glycolysis (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyruvate kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Addition of TEPP-46 for 1 hr to cultured NK cells that had been previously stimulated for 18 hr with IL-2/IL-12 resulted in an increase in cellular glycolysis.
source: As expected, addition of TEPP-46 for 1 hr to cultured NK cells that had been previously stimulated for 18 hr with IL-2/IL-12, resulted in an increase in pyruvate kinase activity and of cellular glycolysis (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data shown in Figure 6b–c.

claim: A substantial portion of PKM2 is present in the less catalytically active mono/dimeric conformation in IL-2/IL-12 stimulated NK cells.
source: These data confirm that a substantial portion of PKM2 is present in the less catalytically active mono/dimeric conformation in IL-2/IL-12 stimulated NK cells, as its enzymatic activity can be boosted by TEPP-46.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TEPP-46 can increase PKM2 enzymatic activity.

claim: NK cells treated with TEPP-46 were viable but showed reduced production of IFNγ.
source: NK cells treated with TEPP-46 were viable but showed reduced production of IFNγ and reduced granzyme B expression (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6d–e.

claim: NK cells treated with TEPP-46 showed reduced granzyme B expression.
source: NK cells treated with TEPP-46 were viable but showed reduced production of IFNγ and reduced granzyme B expression (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: TEPP-46 treated NK cells secreted reduced amounts of TNFα and IL10 while maintaining normal production of MIP1α/β chemokines.
source: TEPP-46 treated NK cells also secreted reduced amounts of TNFα and IL10 while maintaining normal production of MIP1α/β chemokines (Figure 6g–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytometric bead array data shown in Figure 6g–h.

claim: TEPP-46 impaired Pkm2NK-WT IFNγ and granzyme B production while having no effect in Pkm2NK-KO cells.
source: TEPP-46 impaired Pkm2NK-WT IFNγ and granzyme B production while having no effect in Pkm2NK-KO cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TEPP-46 did not affect pyruvate kinase activity in Pkm2NK-KO cells.
source: Similarly, TEPP-46 did not affect pyruvate kinase activity in Pkm2NK-KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pyruvate kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: NK cells stimulated in the presence of TEPP-46 were smaller in size than vehicle-treated NK cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that NK cells stimulated in the presence of TEPP-46 were smaller in size than vehicle-treated NK cells suggesting defects in cellular growth (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry forward scatter data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: TEPP-46-treated NK cells showed reduced proliferation in response to IL2/IL12 stimulation.
source: TEPP-46-treated NK cells also showed reduced proliferation in response to IL2/IL12 stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell trace violet proliferation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In NK cells stimulated with IL-2/IL-12 plus TEPP-46, the basal rates of glycolysis were equivalent to those of NK cells stimulated with IL-2/IL-12 alone.
source: However, NK cells stimulated with IL-2/IL-12 plus TEPP-46, the basal rates of glycolysis were equivalent to those of NK cells stimulated with IL-2/IL-12 alone (Figure 7b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: There was a small but significant effect of TEPP-46 on NK cell glycolytic capacity.
source: There was also a small but significant effect on NK cell glycolytic capacity (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Metabolomics analysis showed no decrease in the levels of glycolytic intermediates in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: While metabolomics analysis showed no decrease in the levels glycolytic intermediates there were decreased levels of the PPP metabolite ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) arguing that in the presence of TEPP-46 glucose-6-phosphate might be withheld from the PPP (Figure 7d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: There were decreased levels of the PPP metabolite ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: While metabolomics analysis showed no decrease in the levels glycolytic intermediates there were decreased levels of the PPP metabolite ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) arguing that in the presence of TEPP-46 glucose-6-phosphate might be withheld from the PPP (Figure 7d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: TEPP-46-treated NK cells showed a dramatic increase in ROS compared to vehicle controls.
source: Indeed, TEPP-46-treated NK cells showed a dramatic increase in ROS compared to vehicle controls, as measured using the flow cytometric ROS probe H2-DCFDA (Figure 8a).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry ROS measurement data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Inhibition of flux through the PPP using the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor, DHEA, resulted in an increase in ROS.
source: Inhibition of flux through the PPP using the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor, DHEA, similarly resulted in an increase in ROS (Figure 8b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry ROS measurement data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the levels of NADPH in TEPP-46-treated NK cells.
source: Accordingly, we found a significant decrease in the levels of NADPH in TEPP-46-treated NK cells (Figure 8c).
evidence: The claim is supported by NADPH assay data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Two of the most significantly upregulated genes in TEPP-46-treated NK cells were members of the metallothionein family, namely Mt1 and Mt2.
source: Moreover, supporting that there was increased oxidative stress in TEPP-46-treated NK cells, our RNAseq data showed that two of the most significantly upregulated genes in TEPP-46-treated NK cells were members of the metallothionein family, namely Mt1 and Mt2 (Figure 8d).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Metallothioneins are a set of zinc-responsive proteins that have antioxidant properties and are known to be induced in response to oxidative stress.
source: Metallothioneins are a set of zinc-responsive proteins that have antioxidant properties and are known to be induced in response to oxidative stress (Ruttkay-Nedecky et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ruttkay-Nedecky et al., 2013.

claim: There was no difference in the membrane potential-dependent mitochondrial mass in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: While there was no difference in the membrane potential-dependent mitochondrial mass in TEPP-46 treated NK cells (Figure 8e), we found that there was a substantial decrease in the basal rates of OXPHOS (Figure 8f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Mitotracker flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: There was a substantial decrease in the basal rates of OXPHOS in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: While there was no difference in the membrane potential-dependent mitochondrial mass in TEPP-46 treated NK cells (Figure 8e), we found that there was a substantial decrease in the basal rates of OXPHOS (Figure 8f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse oxygen consumption rate data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: There was a greatly decreased maximum respiration and spare respiratory capacity in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: Additionally, there was a greatly decreased maximum respiration and spare respiratory capacity (Figure 8g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse oxygen consumption rate data shown in Figure 8g,h.

claim: The metabolites of both the TCA cycle and the Citrate-Malate shuttle were reduced in TEPP-46 treated NK cells.
source: The metabolites of both these cycles were reduced in TEPP-46 treated NK cells (Figure 8i).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 8i.

claim: The levels of glutamine and glutamate were reduced in TEPP-46 treated NK cells, indicative of impaired glutaminolysis.
source: In line with decreased fueling of oxidative metabolism, the levels of glutamine and glutamate were also reduced indicative of impaired glutaminolysis (Figure 8j).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8j.

claim: The transcription factor cMyc was reduced in TEPP-46-treated NK cells at the protein level but not at the transcriptomic level.
source: The transcription factor cMyc is important for glutamine metabolism and was also found to be reduced in TEPP-46-treated NK cells; however, this was only at the protein level as it was not found to be altered in the transcriptomic dataset (Figure 8k).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8k and RNAseq data.

claim: The addition of antioxidant MitoQ was sufficient to partially restore the expression of cMyc protein expression in TEPP-46-treated NK cells.
source: Interestingly, the addition of antioxidant MitoQ was sufficient to partially restore the expression of cMyc protein expression in TEPP-46-treated NK cells (Figure 9a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: The antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) profoundly reduced TEPP-46 induced ROS.
source: We could also profoundly reduce TEPP-46 induced ROS using the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Figure 9b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry ROS measurement data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: NAC treatment could rescue the production of IFNγ, but not that of TNF in NK cells stimulated with IL2/12+TEPP46.
source: In addition, NAC treatment could rescue the production of IFNγ, but not that of TNF in NK cells stimulated with IL2/12+TEPP46 (Figure 9c).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytometric bead array data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: PKM2 is involved in metabolic but not transcriptional regulation of NK cell responses.
source: Taken together, this study demonstrates that PKM2 is involved in metabolic but not transcriptional regulation of NK cell responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined genetic and pharmacological data showing minimal transcriptional changes but significant metabolic effects.

claim: PKM2 has no significant role in regulating HIF1α and STAT associated gene expression in NK cells.
source: Our study shows that PKM2 has no significant role in regulating HIF1α and STAT associated gene expression in NK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq analysis showing no enrichment for HIF1α or STAT target genes in PKM2-deficient or TEPP-46 treated NK cells.

claim: While PKM2 is the most highly expressed isoform in NK cells, either deletion of PKM2 or allosteric tetramerisation of PKM2 has minimal impact upon the NK cell transcriptome.
source: The data clearly show that while PKM2 is the most highly expressed isoform in NK cells, either deletion of PKM2 or allosteric tetramerisation of PKM2 has minimal impact upon the NK cell transcriptome and that there was no evidence of significantly altered expression of HIF1α or STAT target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data from both Pkm2NK-KO and TEPP-46 treated NK cells.

claim: Glycolysis is important for the function of NK cells as inhibition of glycolysis disrupts normal NK cell effector functions including the production of IFNγ and the lysis of target cells.
source: Glycolysis is important for the function of NK cells as inhibition of glycolysis disrupts normal NK cell effector functions including the production of IFNγ and the lysis of target cells (Assmann et al., 2017; Donnelly et al., 2014; Keating et al., 2016; Loftus et al., 2018; Kedia-Mehta et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PKM1 forms a homo tetramer that efficiently converts phosphoenolpyruvate and ADP into pyruvate and ATP.
source: PKM1 forms a homo tetramer that efficiently converts phosphoenolpyruvate and ADP into pyruvate and ATP.
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge about PKM1.

claim: PKM2 can form a catalytically efficient tetramer and is also found as a monomer/dimer that has substantially less catalytic activity.
source: While PKM2 can similarly form a catalytically efficient tetramer, it is also found as a monomer/dimer (called monomeric PKM2 hereafter) that has substantially less catalytic activity (Christofk et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Christofk et al., 2008.

claim: In situations where PKM2 is predominantly mono/dimeric, the rate of glycolytic flux may be slowed leading to an accumulation of upstream glycolytic intermediates that can be diverted into other pathways such as the PPP to support cellular biosynthesis.
source: Therefore, in situations where PKM2 is predominantly mono/dimeric, the rate of glycolytic flux may be slowed leading to an accumulation of upstream glycolytic intermediates that can be diverted into other pathways such as the PPP to support cellular biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established metabolic principles and inference from PKM2 biochemistry.

claim: PKM2 expression has been found to be elevated in many cells with high biosynthetic burdens including tumour cells.
source: Accordingly, PKM2 expression has been found to be elevated in many cells with high biosynthetic burdens including tumour cells (Li et al., 2018; Hitosugi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Hitosugi et al., 2009.

claim: Monomeric PKM2 has functions independent of its metabolic role in glycolysis, primarily in the nucleus where it contributes to transcriptional control through interactions with HIF-1α and STAT transcription factors.
source: Monomeric PKM2 has also been shown to have functions independent of its metabolic role in glycolysis, primarily in the nucleus where it contributes to transcriptional control through interactions with the hypoxia inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and signal transduction and activator of transcription (STAT) transcription factors (Hitosugi et al., 2009; Demaria and Poli, 2012; Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hitosugi et al., 2009; Demaria and Poli, 2012; Dong et al., 2016.

claim: Mono/dimeric PKM2 is converted to the catalytically efficient tetramer when levels of upstream metabolites such as fructose-1,6-phosphate or serine are high.

claim: IL-15 is a cytokine required for DC-mediated NK cell priming in vivo.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lucas et al., 2007; Dubois et al., 2002; Koka et al., 2004.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2019; Keating et al., 2016; Kedia-Mehta et al., 2019.

claim: PKM2-regulated glycolytic metabolism and redox status, not transcriptional control, facilitate optimal NK cell responses.

claim: Acute pharmacological activation of PKM2 catalytic activity blunted NK cell growth and effector functions.
source: In contrast, acute pharmacological activation of PKM2 catalytic activity blunted NK cell growth and effector functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments with TEPP-46 showing reduced cell size, proliferation, and cytokine production.

claim: Defects in NK cell function caused by TEPP-46 were associated with increased levels of ROS and a transcriptional signature indicating oxidative stress.
source: These defects were associated with increased levels of ROS and a transcriptional signature indicating oxidative stress that we linked to reduced PPP metabolites and decreased NADPH levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS measurements, RNAseq data showing Mt1/Mt2 upregulation, and NADPH measurements.

claim: TEPP-46-induced defects in NK cell function were linked to reduced PPP metabolites and decreased NADPH levels.
source: These defects were associated with increased levels of ROS and a transcriptional signature indicating oxidative stress that we linked to reduced PPP metabolites and decreased NADPH levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data showing reduced ribose-5-phosphate and NADPH measurements.

claim: This study reveals an important metabolic role for PKM2 in supporting the PPP and redox balance in activated NK cells.
source: Overall, this study reveals an important metabolic role for PKM2 in supporting the PPP and redox balance in activated NK cells and highlights that PKM2 does not have a profound transcriptional role in all immune cells.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion inferred from the TEPP-46 experiments showing effects on PPP metabolites, NADPH, and ROS.

claim: PKM2 does not have a profound transcriptional role in all immune cells.
source: Overall, this study reveals an important metabolic role for PKM2 in supporting the PPP and redox balance in activated NK cells and highlights that PKM2 does not have a profound transcriptional role in all immune cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the contrast between the lack of transcriptional effects in NK cells versus reported transcriptional effects in other immune cells.
